questions.question: A returning patient has a post-fracture wound growing an Acinetobacter resistant to essentially all antibiotics.
questions.question_raw: Returning patient with an Acinetobacter resistant to everything in a post fracture wound.

parts.text: Indicate two mechanisms of resistance to carbapenems.
Give two alternatives for antibiotic treatment.

parts_raw.text: Indicate two mechanisms of resistance to carbapenems
Give two alternatives for antibiotic treatment

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Carbapenem-hydrolyzing enzymes: Ambler class D oxacillinases (intrinsic OXA-51-like and acquired OXA subclasses on chromosome/plasmids) and class B metallo-beta-lactamases (IMP, VIM, NDM). (2) Efflux pumps of the RND family (predominantly AdeABC) which expel beta-lactams and carbapenems; reduced outer membrane permeability via loss/alteration of the OmpAab porin also contributes.
b) (1) Sulbactam (alone or as ampicillin-sulbactam), the most active beta-lactamase inhibitor against Acinetobacter, at >=4 g/day. (2) A polymyxin (colistin or polymyxin B); tigecycline is an additional option.

cohort_answer.text:
Two mechanisms of resistance: Carbapenemase production; Efflux pump; Change in PBPs
Two alternatives: Colistin; Tigecycline

questions.question: Multidrug-resistant Acinetobacter.

parts.text: What is the mechanism of carbapenem resistance?
What is the preferred treatment if carbapenems cannot be used?

parts_raw.text: a) What is the mechanism of carbapenem resistance?
b) What is the preferred treatment if carbapenems cannot be used?

questions.model_answer:
a) The principal mechanism is production of carbapenem-hydrolyzing class D oxacillinases (group 2d Ambler class D): the intrinsic, chromosomal OXA-51-like enzyme (over-expressed when driven by the ISAba1 promoter) plus acquired OXA subclasses (e.g., OXA-23-like) on chromosome and plasmids; less commonly class B metallo-beta-lactamases (IMP, VIM, NDM). Efflux pumps (AdeABC/RND) and porin (OmpAab) loss reduce drug access.
b) Sulbactam (ampicillin-sulbactam, >=4 g sulbactam/day) is the preferred agent when susceptible; polymyxins (colistin/polymyxin B) and tigecycline are alternatives, and cefiderocol is effective against extensively resistant strains. Combination therapy and extended/continuous beta-lactam infusion may be used.

cohort_answer.text:
OXA-51 Carbapenemase – intrinsic/chromosomal, often expressed poorly. Efflux pump also common (resistance to B-lactam, chloramphenicol, macrolides, tetracycline, aminoglycosides). Acquired carbapenemases: Ambler Class B MBL (emerging): IMP (plasmids), VIM (more common), NDM; OXA-48 (Class D)
Rate of MDR <10-15% and not critical illness: cefepime 2g IV q8h or meropenem 2g IV q8h infused over 3 hrs. Rate of MDR >10-15% and/or critical illness: consider combo of amp-sulbactam + mero + polymyxin B (can also use colistin and tige)

parts.text: What are two mechanisms that lead to carbapenem resistance?
What two treatment options can be used?

parts_raw.text: a) What are 2 mechanisms that lead to carbapenem resistance?
b) What 2 tx options can be used?

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Carbapenem-hydrolyzing enzymes: Ambler class D oxacillinases (intrinsic OXA-51-like and acquired OXA subclasses on chromosome/plasmids) and class B metallo-beta-lactamases (IMP, VIM, NDM). (2) Efflux pumps (RND family, AdeABC) plus reduced permeability from loss of the OmpAab porin.
b) (1) Sulbactam (ampicillin-sulbactam). (2) A polymyxin (colistin or polymyxin B); tigecycline and cefiderocol are additional options, and extended-infusion beta-lactams or combination therapy may be considered.

cohort_answer.text: a) Beta-lactamases hydrolyzing carbapenems: Ambler class D oxacillinases (OXAs) group 2d (OXA-51-like intrinsic/chromosomal; acquired OXA subclasses on chromosomes/plasmids, zinc-dependent metalloenzymes); intrinsic class B beta-lactamases (Stenotrophomonas maltophilia, Elizabethkingia meningoseptica); acquired class B beta-lactamases (VIM, NDM); Ambler Class A beta-lactamases (KPCs). Also porins (diminished permeability from impaired OMP expression) and efflux of drugs across outer membrane. b) Tigecycline or Minocycline; Colistin or polymyxin B; continuous/extended intermittent beta-lactam infusion; local instillation of colistin (intrathecal for CNS); combination therapy (colistin + minocycline/tigecycline/carbapenem/rifampin); newer agents (ceftazidime-avibactam, ceftolozane-tazobactam, meropenem-vaborbactam, imipenem-cilastatin-relebactam, plazomicin, eravacycline, cefiderocol, IV fosfomycin).

parts.text: What drugs can you use to treat?

parts_raw.text: What drugs can you use to treat?

questions.model_answer:
a) Acinetobacter baumannii (multidrug/extensively drug-resistant war-wound infection).
b) (1) Sulbactam (high-dose ampicillin-sulbactam). (2) A polymyxin (colistin or polymyxin B). (3) Tigecycline or cefiderocol; extended/continuous beta-lactam infusion, local instillation of colistin, and combination therapy are adjuncts.

cohort_answer.text: Acinetobacter baumannii. Treatment: High dose amp-sulbactam, Tigecycline/minocycline, Colistin/polymyxin B; rifamycins not recommended (insufficient evidence); extended infusion meropenem (combined with other agents), local instillation, phage therapy

questions.question: For tigecycline, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (Septra), and imipenem, indicate which of Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Acinetobacter species, and Stenotrophomonas maltophilia are intrinsically resistant to which agents.
questions.question_raw: Tigecycline, Septra, imipenem vs Acinetobacter, Pseudomonas, Stenotrophomonas.  Which bugs are intrinsically resistant to which agents?

parts.text: State the intrinsic resistance of Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter, and Stenotrophomonas to tigecycline, TMP-SMX, and imipenem.

parts_raw.text: Which bugs are intrinsically resistant to which agents? (Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter, Stenotrophomonas)

questions.model_answer: Pseudomonas aeruginosa: resistant to tigecycline (intrinsic), resistant to TMP-SMX (intrinsic), susceptible to imipenem. Acinetobacter spp.: susceptible/active for tigecycline, TMP-SMX, and imipenem (no intrinsic resistance to these three, though acquired resistance is common). Stenotrophomonas maltophilia: susceptible to tigecycline, susceptible to TMP-SMX (drug of choice), intrinsically resistant to imipenem/all carbapenems (chromosomal L1 metallo-beta-lactamase).
questions.beyond_mandell: Intrinsic-resistance profiles per CLSI/EUCAST and Mandell; Stenotrophomonas carbapenem resistance from the L1 MBL.

cohort_answer.text:
Pseudo: R- Tigecycline, R- Septra, S-Imipenem
Acinetobacter: S- Septra, S- tige, S- Imi
Steno: R- Imipenem, S- tigecycline, S- Septra

questions.question: Antibacterial mechanisms of resistance. For each organism, indicate susceptible (S) or resistant (R) to tigecycline, ertapenem, and colistin: Acinetobacter, Stenotrophomonas, Pseudomonas, Proteus, and ESBL-producing Escherichia coli.
questions.question_raw: Q45 (2012 AM). Antibacterial Mechanism of Resistance. Chart to fill in (R or S): | Tigecycline | Ertapenem | Colistin for Acinetobacter, Stenotrophomonas, Pseudomonas, Proteus, ESBL
questions.model_answer:
Tigecycline | Ertapenem | Colistin
Acinetobacter: S | R | S
Stenotrophomonas: S | R | S
Pseudomonas: R | R | S
Proteus: R | S | R
ESBL E. coli: S | S | S
Key intrinsic points: tigecycline lacks reliable activity against Pseudomonas and Proteus/Providencia/Morganella; ertapenem has no antipseudomonal activity and is unreliable for Acinetobacter, and Stenotrophomonas is intrinsically carbapenem-resistant (L1 metallo-beta-lactamase); colistin is inactive against Proteus (also Serratia, Providencia, Morganella) which are intrinsically polymyxin-resistant.
questions.beyond_mandell: Intrinsic-resistance patterns are from CLSI intrinsic-resistance tables and Mandell Ch. 18 (antimicrobial resistance), not this chapter.

cohort_answer.text: Acinetobacter | S | R | S. Stenotrophomonas | S | R | S. Pseudomonas | R | R | S. Proteus | R | S | R. ESBL | S | S | S.
